rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
(a) Give any two differences between order and molecularity of a reaction.
(b) For a reaction \(\mathrm{X} + \mathrm{Y} \rightarrow \mathrm{Z}\), in which both X and Y follow first order kinetics; if the concentration of X is increased 2 times and concentration of Y is increased 3 times, how does it affect the rate of reaction ?
rows.solution:
(a) Two differences:
ORDER is an EXPERIMENTAL quantity, read off the measured rate law, whereas MOLECULARITY is a THEORETICAL one, read off the mechanism as the number of species colliding in an elementary step.
ORDER applies to elementary and complex reactions alike, whereas MOLECULARITY is defined only for elementary reactions — a multi-step reaction has no single collision to count.
A third difference follows from these: order may be zero or fractional, while molecularity must be a whole number and at least 1.

(b) Both reactants are first order, so the rate law is
\(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{X}][\mathrm{Y}]\)

Doubling \([\mathrm{X}]\) and trebling \([\mathrm{Y}]\) gives
\(\text{new rate} = k(2[\mathrm{X}])(3[\mathrm{Y}]) = 6\,k[\mathrm{X}][\mathrm{Y}]\)

The rate increases SIX times. The two factors multiply rather than add, because each concentration enters the rate law as its own separate power.

rows.stem: Write the mechanism of dehydration of ethyl alcohol with conc. \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) at 443 K.
rows.solution:
At 443 K — the HIGHER of the two dehydration temperatures — ethanol gives ETHENE. The mechanism has three steps.

Step 1 — formation of the protonated alcohol. The oxygen uses a lone pair to pick up a proton from the acid. This step is fast and reversible:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-OH} + \mathrm{H^+} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3CH_2-\overset{+}{O}H_2}\)
The product is the ethyl oxonium ion.

Step 2 — formation of the carbocation. The protonated alcohol loses a molecule of water. This is the SLOW step and therefore the rate-determining one, because a bond breaks and a charged species is created:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-\overset{+}{O}H_2} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3-\overset{+}{C}H_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Step 3 — elimination of a proton. A base removes a proton from the carbon next to the positive centre, and the pair of electrons left behind forms the double bond, regenerating the catalyst:
\(\mathrm{CH_3-\overset{+}{C}H_2} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2} + \mathrm{H^+}\)

The temperature selects the product: at 413 K a second alcohol molecule attacks the protonated one instead, and the product is ethoxyethane.

rows.stem:
(a) Carboxylic acid is more acidic than phenol. Give reason.
(b) Give a chemical test to distinguish between benzaldehyde and acetophenone.
rows.solution:
(a) Because the CARBOXYLATE ion is better stabilised than the phenoxide ion. When a carboxylic acid loses its proton the negative charge is delocalised over TWO equivalent oxygen atoms — two identical resonance structures, with the charge shared equally between two electronegative atoms. When phenol loses its proton the charge is delocalised into the benzene RING, onto carbon atoms, which are far less electronegative and hold it less comfortably; and the resonance structures are not equivalent. The more stable the anion, the more readily the proton leaves, so the carboxylic acid is the stronger acid.

(b) Use the IODOFORM test. Warm each with sodium hydroxide and iodine: acetophenone carries a \(\mathrm{CH_3CO-}\) group and gives a yellow precipitate of iodoform; benzaldehyde has no methyl on its carbonyl and gives none.

Tollens' reagent would serve equally well the other way round — benzaldehyde is an aldehyde and gives a silver mirror, while acetophenone, a ketone, does not.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the name and structure of a hexadentate ligand.
(b) Why is \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}\) square planar while \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) is tetrahedral ?
[Atomic number : Ni = 28]
rows.solution:
(a) The hexadentate ligand is the ETHYLENEDIAMINETETRAACETATE ion, \(\mathrm{EDTA^{4-}}\).

Its structure is a two-carbon bridge, \(-\mathrm{CH_2CH_2}-\), joining two nitrogen atoms, and each nitrogen carries two \(-\mathrm{CH_2COO^-}\) arms:
\((^-\mathrm{OOC-CH_2})_2\mathrm{N-CH_2-CH_2-N(CH_2-COO^-})_2\)
It binds a metal ion through SIX donor atoms at once — the two nitrogens and one oxygen from each of the four carboxylate arms — wrapping right around the ion and closing five chelate rings, which is why its complexes are so exceptionally stable.

(b) The two differ in the OXIDATION STATE of the nickel, not just in the ligand.

In \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}\) nickel is \(+2\), so \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\). Cyanide is a strong field ligand and forces the two unpaired electrons to pair, freeing ONE \(3d\) orbital; that orbital with the \(4s\) and two \(4p\) gives \(dsp^2\) hybridisation and a SQUARE PLANAR geometry.

In \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) nickel is in the ZERO oxidation state, \(3d^8 4s^2\). Carbon monoxide drives the \(4s\) electrons into the \(3d\) set, giving \(3d^{10}\) with no \(3d\) orbital free at all; bonding must then use the \(4s\) and all three \(4p\) orbitals, giving \(sp^3\) hybridisation and a TETRAHEDRAL geometry.

rows.stem:
Account for the following :
(a) Haloarenes are less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution reactions.
(b) p-dichlorobenzene has higher melting point than ortho and meta isomers.
(c) Tertiary alkyl halides are least reactive towards \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction.
rows.solution:
(a) Three reasons, all pulling the same way. The lone pair on the halogen is delocalised into the ring, so the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond acquires partial double bond character, becomes shorter and stronger, and resists breaking. The carbon carrying the halogen is \(sp^2\) rather than \(sp^3\), and an \(sp^2\) carbon is more electronegative and holds the shared pair more tightly. And the electron-rich \(\pi\) cloud of the ring repels the approaching nucleophile. The phenyl cation that a unimolecular route would require is also highly unstable.

(b) The para isomer is the most SYMMETRICAL of the three, so its molecules pack into the crystal lattice more closely and more regularly. A better packed lattice takes more energy to break down, so p-dichlorobenzene melts highest. Note the argument concerns the SOLID state only: boiling points follow dipole moment instead, and there the para isomer, being non-polar, comes out lowest.

(c) Because an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction requires the nucleophile to attack the carbon from the side directly OPPOSITE the leaving group, and a tertiary carbon is surrounded by three alkyl groups that block that approach almost completely. Steric hindrance, not electronics, is what slows it. A tertiary halide instead reacts by \(\mathrm{S_N}1\), where the same three alkyl groups HELP, by stabilising the carbocation — which is why the two orders are exactly reversed.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the chemical equation for the following :
(i) Preparation of phenol from cumene
(ii) Nitration of anisole
(b) Complete the following :
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\,\mathrm{C} - \mathrm{O} - \mathrm{CH_3} + \mathrm{HI} \rightarrow\)
rows.solution:
(a)(i) Phenol from cumene. Cumene is oxidised by air to cumene hydroperoxide, and treating that with dilute acid cleaves it into phenol and acetone — the industrial route, valuable because both products are useful.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH(CH_3)_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{O_2}} \mathrm{C_6H_5C(CH_3)_2OOH} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\)

(ii) Nitration of anisole. The \(-\mathrm{OCH_3}\) group is activating and ortho, para directing, so a mixture of the two isomers is obtained, the para predominating:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OCH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{HNO_3}/\mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \text{2-nitroanisole} + \text{4-nitroanisole}\)

(b) Cleavage of an ether by hydrogen iodide, with one group tertiary, takes the unimolecular route: the protonated ether breaks to give the relatively stable tertiary carbocation, which the iodide then captures. So the iodine goes to the TERTIARY carbon and the methyl group keeps the oxygen:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-O-CH_3} + \mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-I} + \mathrm{CH_3OH}\)
Had both groups been primary the mechanism would have been bimolecular and the iodide would have attacked the LESS hindered carbon instead.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Write the products formed in the following reactions :
(a) \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} + \mathrm{NH_2CONHNH_2} \rightarrow\)
(b) \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. NaOH}}\)
(c) \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{Cl_2/red\,P}}\)
rows.solution:
(a) Semicarbazide condenses with the carbonyl group, losing water, to give the semicarbazone:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} + \mathrm{NH_2CONHNH_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}N-NHCONH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

(b) Dilute alkali brings about an ALDOL ADDITION between two molecules of ethanal: the carbanion from one attacks the carbonyl of the other, giving the \(\beta\)-hydroxy aldehyde. Without heating it stops there:
\(2\mathrm{CH_3CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CHO}\)
Heating would dehydrate this to but-2-enal.

(c) This is the Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction: chlorine with a little red phosphorus halogenates the acid at the \(\alpha\) position, and hydrolysis gives the \(\alpha\)-chloro acid:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{Cl_2}/\text{red P}} \mathrm{ClCH_2COOH}\)
The product is chloroethanoic acid, a markedly stronger acid than the one it came from.

rows.stem:
(a) Name the vitamin which is responsible for coagulation of blood.
(b) What is meant by denaturation of protein ? Give an example.
rows.solution:
(a) Vitamin K is responsible for the coagulation of blood; its deficiency causes increased clotting time.

(b) Denaturation is the loss of a protein's BIOLOGICAL ACTIVITY when its native structure is destroyed by a physical or chemical change — heating, or a change in pH. The hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions holding the chain in shape are disrupted, so the helix uncoils and the globule unfolds: the SECONDARY and TERTIARY structures are destroyed while the PRIMARY structure, the sequence of residues, survives intact because no peptide bond is broken.

Example: coagulation of egg white on boiling. Curdling of milk is another.
